name: Psychedelic Rock
blurb: San Francisco ballrooms, 12-string ragas and the long, strange trip of the Grateful Dead.

questions.prompt: What were the Grateful Dead called before they changed their name in late 1965?
questions.fact: They learned another band already used the name. Jerry Garcia found the phrase "grateful dead" in a dictionary.

questions.prompt: Besides "Somebody to Love", which Surrealistic Pillow song became a 1967 top 10 hit for Jefferson Airplane?
questions.fact: "Somebody to Love" reached number 5 and "White Rabbit" number 8, and the album climbed to number 3.

questions.prompt: Grace Slick brought "Somebody to Love" and "White Rabbit" to Jefferson Airplane from which band?
choices: Big Brother and the Holding Company
questions.fact: "Somebody to Love" was written by her brother-in-law, Darby Slick, who played guitar in the Great Society.

questions.prompt: "White Rabbit" takes its imagery from which book?
questions.fact: Slick built its slow crescendo with Ravel's Bolero and Miles Davis's Sketches of Spain in mind.

questions.prompt: Who played lead guitar in Jefferson Airplane?
questions.fact: Kaukonen and bassist Jack Casady also formed Hot Tuna, which began as a side project in 1969.

questions.prompt: The Byrds said "Eight Miles High" was about what, though radio stations heard drug references?
questions.fact: It described their 1965 flight to London and English tour. Years later David Crosby admitted it was a drug song too.

questions.prompt: Roger McGuinn's chiming Byrds sound came from which guitar?
questions.fact: He took it up after seeing George Harrison play one in A Hard Day's Night.

questions.prompt: Which member was fired from the Byrds in 1967 and soon joined Crosby, Stills & Nash?
questions.fact: McGuinn and Hillman let him go in October 1967. The Crosby, Stills & Nash debut came out in 1969.

questions.prompt: Which 1966 Byrds album includes "Eight Miles High"?
questions.fact: Gene Clark, the song's main writer, left the band in March 1966, months before the album came out.

questions.prompt: Which Grateful Dead sound man, nicknamed Bear, led the design of the band's 1974 Wall of Sound?
questions.fact: Before that he was one of the best-known makers of LSD in California. The Wall was retired after the Dead's October 1974 Winterland shows.

questions.prompt: Ken Kesey's 1965-66 parties, where the Grateful Dead were the house band, were called what?
questions.fact: Kesey's posters asked "Can you pass the acid test?", and Tom Wolfe told the story in The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test (1968).

questions.prompt: Which 1970 Grateful Dead album includes "Truckin'", "Ripple" and "Sugar Magnolia"?
questions.fact: It came out in November 1970, only five months after Workingman's Dead.

questions.prompt: Who wrote the lyrics for most of Jerry Garcia's Grateful Dead songs?
questions.fact: Barlow wrote mainly with Bob Weir. Hunter was the only non-performer inducted with the band into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

questions.prompt: Janis Joplin sang with which San Francisco band at the 1967 Monterey Pop Festival?
choices: Big Brother and the Holding Company
questions.fact: Their manager refused to let them be filmed on Saturday, so the band played again on Sunday for D.A. Pennebaker's cameras.

questions.prompt: Which underground cartoonist drew the cover of Big Brother and the Holding Company's Cheap Thrills?
questions.fact: Crumb meant it for the back cover, but Joplin insisted it go on the front. The album spent eight weeks at number one in 1968.

questions.prompt: Country Joe McDonald led the Woodstock crowd in the Fish Cheer before which anti-war song?
questions.fact: At Woodstock he spelled out a four-letter word instead of F-I-S-H.

questions.prompt: Iron Butterfly's "In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida" fills a whole album side and runs about how long?
questions.fact: The title is usually explained as singer Doug Ingle's slurred "In the Garden of Eden".

questions.prompt: What did Tommy Hall play in the 13th Floor Elevators?
questions.fact: The Austin band's 1966 debut, The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators, was among the first albums to put "psychedelic" in its title.

questions.prompt: Who sang the 13th Floor Elevators' "You're Gonna Miss Me"?
questions.fact: Erickson had first recorded the song with his earlier band, the Spades.

questions.prompt: Which Los Angeles band, led by Arthur Lee, made the 1967 album Forever Changes?
questions.fact: It peaked at only number 154 in America but reached number 24 in Britain, and its reputation has grown ever since.

questions.prompt: Columbia released how many singles from Moby Grape's 1967 debut on the same day?
questions.fact: Ten of the album's 13 songs came out at once in June 1967, and the stunt got the band branded as hype.

questions.prompt: Skip Spence played drums on Jefferson Airplane's first album before co-founding which band?
questions.fact: He was really a guitarist. His only solo album, Oar (1969), became a cult favorite.

questions.prompt: Whose quivering, vibrato-heavy guitar defined Quicksilver Messenger Service?
questions.fact: Their 1969 album Happy Trails was recorded mostly live at the Fillmore East and Fillmore West.

questions.prompt: Which promoter ran the Fillmore Auditorium in San Francisco and later the Fillmore East in New York?
questions.fact: His first shows were 1965 benefits for the San Francisco Mime Troupe, which he managed.

questions.prompt: Chet Helms and the Family Dog put on shows at which San Francisco ballroom?
questions.fact: Helms also helped bring Janis Joplin from Texas into Big Brother and the Holding Company.

questions.prompt: The Human Be-In of January 1967 was held in which San Francisco park?
questions.fact: Timothy Leary urged the crowd to "turn on, tune in, drop out", and the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane played.

questions.prompt: Which San Francisco neighborhood was the center of 1967's Summer of Love?
questions.fact: The Grateful Dead lived at 710 Ashbury Street, a few blocks from the corner that gives the district its name.

questions.prompt: Who wrote Scott McKenzie's 1967 hit "San Francisco (Be Sure to Wear Flowers in Your Hair)"?
questions.fact: Phillips wrote it to promote the Monterey Pop Festival, which he helped organize.

questions.prompt: At Altamont in December 1969, which band was on the bill but left without playing?
questions.fact: They left after hearing that Marty Balin had been knocked out by a Hells Angel during Jefferson Airplane's set.

questions.prompt: Which 1987 song was the Grateful Dead's only top 10 hit?
questions.fact: It reached number 9 on the Billboard Hot 100 and came from the album In the Dark.

questions.prompt: In 1984 the Grateful Dead set aside a section at their shows for fans doing what?
questions.fact: The band let fans tape and trade its shows as long as nobody sold the recordings.

questions.prompt: Jerry Garcia lost two-thirds of which finger in a childhood accident?
questions.fact: His older brother cut it off by accident while they were splitting wood in the Santa Cruz Mountains. Jerry was four.

questions.prompt: Jerry Garcia's parents named him after which composer?
questions.fact: His father, Jose Garcia, was a bandleader and clarinetist.

questions.prompt: Which founding Grateful Dead member, the band's blues singer and organist, was known as Pigpen?
questions.fact: He sang "Turn On Your Love Light" and "Good Lovin'", and he died in March 1973 at 27.

questions.prompt: Who joined Bill Kreutzmann in 1967 to give the Grateful Dead two drummers?
questions.fact: Hart left in 1971 and came back in 1974.

questions.prompt: Which Grateful Dead member studied composition with Luciano Berio before joining the band?
questions.fact: He had played trumpet and violin, and took up bass guitar only when Garcia asked him to join the Warlocks.

questions.prompt: Jefferson Airplane's 1968 Manhattan rooftop concert was filmed for a project begun by which French director?
questions.fact: Police stopped the unpermitted show and arrested Marty Balin. The Beatles played their rooftop concert two months later.

questions.prompt: Marty Balin formed Jefferson Airplane as the house band for which San Francisco club he helped open in 1965?
questions.fact: The band played the club's opening night on August 13, 1965.

questions.prompt: Who sang with Jefferson Airplane on their first album, before Grace Slick joined?
questions.fact: She left in October 1966 after the birth of her daughter, and Slick played her first show with the band the next night.

questions.prompt: Which song appears on both Jefferson Airplane's Volunteers and the debut album of Crosby, Stills & Nash?
questions.fact: David Crosby, Stephen Stills and Paul Kantner wrote it together in 1968.

questions.prompt: The Doors took their name from which Aldous Huxley book?
questions.fact: Huxley borrowed the phrase from William Blake: "If the doors of perception were cleansed..."

questions.prompt: Pink Floyd's 1967 debut, The Piper at the Gates of Dawn, takes its title from a chapter of which book?
questions.fact: They made it at EMI's Abbey Road studios in 1967 while the Beatles were recording Sgt. Pepper there.

questions.prompt: Pink Floyd's first single, "Arnold Layne", is about a man who steals what?
questions.fact: Roger Waters said it was based on real thefts in Cambridge, where he and Syd Barrett grew up.

questions.prompt: John Lennon took lines for "Tomorrow Never Knows" from a book based on which ancient text?
choices: The Egyptian Book of the Dead
The Tibetan Book of the Dead
questions.fact: The book was The Psychedelic Experience by Timothy Leary, Ralph Metzner and Richard Alpert. The song closes Revolver.

questions.prompt: Matthew Fisher's organ line on Procol Harum's "A Whiter Shade of Pale" echoes which composer?
questions.fact: In 2009 the House of Lords ruled that Fisher was entitled to a share of the songwriting credit.

questions.prompt: Which Los Angeles band reached the top 20 in 1967 with "I Had Too Much to Dream (Last Night)"?
questions.fact: Songwriters Annette Tucker and Nancie Mantz wrote it, not the band.

questions.prompt: Sky Saxon sang "Pushin' Too Hard" with which band?
questions.fact: Some stations banned it, thinking the title was about drug dealing. It reached number 36 in February 1967.

questions.prompt: Spirit's shaved-headed drummer Ed Cassidy was what relation to guitarist Randy California?
questions.fact: Jimi Hendrix gave Randy his stage name when they played together in New York in 1966.

questions.prompt: Which pair drew the Grateful Dead's skull-and-roses artwork?
choices: Robert Crumb and S. Clay Wilson
questions.fact: They adapted an Edmund J. Sullivan illustration from an edition of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam.

questions.prompt: Which psychiatrist introduced the word "psychedelic" to the scientific world in 1957?
questions.fact: He had tried it out in letters with Aldous Huxley, whose first mescaline trip Osmond supervised in 1953.

questions.prompt: Which 1965 Beatles song was their first to feature George Harrison on sitar?
questions.fact: He first came across the instrument on the set of Help! and later studied with Ravi Shankar.

questions.prompt: Before the Warlocks, Garcia, Bob Weir and Pigpen played in which jug band?
questions.fact: Garcia was teaching guitar and banjo around Palo Alto at the time.

songs.title: White Rabbit
songs.note: Grace Slick first sang it with the Great Society; the Airplane cut it to about two and a half minutes.

songs.title: Somebody to Love
songs.note: Written by Darby Slick, Grace's brother-in-law, it reached number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100.

songs.title: Eight Miles High
songs.note: McGuinn's 12-string break was his attempt to play like John Coltrane's saxophone.

songs.title: Truckin'
songs.note: Its line "what a long, strange trip it's been" became the band's unofficial motto.

songs.title: Casey Jones
songs.note: Robert Hunter turned the old railroad ballad into a song about cocaine.

songs.title: Touch of Grey
songs.note: The band had played it live since 1982, five years before the studio version.

songs.title: Ball and Chain
songs.note: Big Mama Thornton wrote it. It was the only track on Cheap Thrills actually recorded live, at Winterland.

songs.title: In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida
songs.note: The single cut the 17-minute album track to under three minutes.

songs.title: You're Gonna Miss Me
songs.album: The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators
songs.note: Tommy Hall's electric jug makes the bubbling sound under the guitar.

songs.title: Alone Again Or
songs.note: Guitarist Bryan MacLean wrote it, one of only two songs on the album not by Arthur Lee.

songs.title: I Had Too Much to Dream (Last Night)
songs.note: The swooping sound at the start is a guitar part played backward, an accident the producer kept.

songs.title: Astronomy Domine
songs.album: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn

songs.title: A Whiter Shade of Pale
songs.note: The band's first single, it topped the UK chart for six weeks.

songs.title: I Got a Line on You
songs.note: Randy California wrote it, and it became the band's biggest single.

songs.title: Omaha
songs.note: Skip Spence wrote it, and it was one of five singles Columbia released from the album on the same day.

songs.title: Time Has Come Today
songs.note: The album version runs 11 minutes. The edited single spent five weeks at number 11 in 1968.

songs.title: Scarlet Begonias
songs.note: Robert Hunter's lyric opens in London's Grosvenor Square. From 1977 the band almost always segued it into "Fire on the Mountain".

songs.title: Incense and Peppermints
songs.note: It reached number one in 1967, sung by Greg Munford, a 16-year-old friend of the band.

stories.title: The Acid Tests
stories.dek: How a jug band became the Grateful Dead
stories.body:
In 1964 Jerry Garcia was a banjo player and guitar teacher in Palo Alto, California, playing bluegrass and jug band music with friends. One of those groups, Mother McCree's Uptown Jug Champions, included a teenage guitarist named Bob Weir and a blues singer and harmonica player named Ron McKernan, whom everyone called Pigpen. Early in 1965 they plugged in, added drummer Bill Kreutzmann, and called themselves the Warlocks. Phil Lesh, a classically trained trumpeter who had studied composition, learned bass to join them.

The name did not last. Another band was already using it, and late in 1965 Garcia opened a dictionary and found the phrase "grateful dead". The others were not sure at first, but it stuck.

The setting that shaped them was a series of parties run by the novelist Ken Kesey, author of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, and his friends the Merry Pranksters. Kesey called them Acid Tests, and his posters asked a simple question: "Can you pass the acid test?" LSD was still legal in California, and the Pranksters handed it out freely. The first Acid Test took place near Santa Cruz in late November 1965. A week later, at an Acid Test in San Jose, the band played for the first time as the Grateful Dead.

There was no stage in the usual sense and no set list. The Pranksters ran tape loops and light projections, Neal Cassady talked nonstop, and the band played for as long as the night lasted. It was chaotic and often went badly. But it taught the Dead to stretch a song out, follow one another and improvise in front of a crowd, habits that defined them for the next 30 years.

The Acid Tests also brought them a patron. Owsley Stanley, an engineer and LSD chemist known as Bear, began bankrolling the band and running its sound, the start of an obsession with audio quality that led to the Wall of Sound in 1974.

In January 1966 the Dead played the three-day Trips Festival at Longshoremen's Hall in San Francisco, which put the Acid Test idea in front of thousands of people. California outlawed LSD that October. By then the Dead had moved into a house in Haight-Ashbury, and the scene that would become the Summer of Love was taking shape around them. Tom Wolfe's book The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test, published in 1968, made the parties famous long after they had ended.

stories.title: Eight Miles High
stories.dek: The Byrds leave folk rock behind
stories.body:
In 1965 the Byrds were the most successful band in American folk rock. Their electric version of Bob Dylan's "Mr. Tambourine Man" went to number one, and "Turn! Turn! Turn!" followed it to the top before the year was out. The sound was Roger McGuinn's Rickenbacker 12-string, which he had taken up after seeing George Harrison play one in A Hard Day's Night, under the band's close harmonies.

That August the band flew to England for a tour that did not go well. The British press was unkind, the venues were wrong for them, and the long flight home gave them time to think. Gene Clark, the band's main songwriter, began a song about the trip, and McGuinn and David Crosby helped finish it. The title came from the height of the plane, which was really closer to six miles up, but "eight" sang better.

The music came from somewhere else. On tour the band had been playing recordings by John Coltrane and the Indian sitar master Ravi Shankar over and over. When the Byrds recorded "Eight Miles High" in Hollywood in January 1966, McGuinn opened it with a jagged 12-string solo that was his attempt to play like Coltrane's saxophone. Chris Hillman's droning bass line and the band's vocal harmonies gave it the sound of a raga. There is no sitar on the record, but many listeners assumed there was.

Columbia released the single in March 1966. Within weeks the Gavin Report, a newsletter that radio programmers relied on, suggested that the lyrics were about drugs, and stations in several states stopped playing it. The band insisted it was about the flight to London, and their publicist backed them. Years later Crosby admitted it was both.

The song peaked at number 14, short of the band's earlier hits. Some writers blame the ban, while others point to its length and how strange it sounded on AM radio next to everything else. By the time it charted, Clark had left the band, worn down by touring and his fear of flying.

The Byrds included it on Fifth Dimension that July, and it is now regarded as one of the first psychedelic rock records. It showed that a pop band could bring jazz and Indian music into a three-minute single, and San Francisco bands were listening closely.

stories.title: Surrealistic Pillow
stories.body:
Jefferson Airplane began in the summer of 1965 as the house band at the Matrix, a small club in San Francisco's Marina district that singer Marty Balin had helped open. Balin recruited Paul Kantner, a folk singer, and Jorma Kaukonen, a blues guitarist. Jack Casady, a friend of Kaukonen's from Washington, D.C., came west to play bass. Their first album, Jefferson Airplane Takes Off, came out in 1966 with Signe Anderson singing beside Balin.

That fall Anderson left the band to raise her baby daughter. Her replacement was Grace Slick, a former model who had been singing with another local group, the Great Society. Slick played her first show with the Airplane in October 1966, the night after Anderson's last. She brought two songs from the Great Society with her. One, "Somebody to Love", had been written by her brother-in-law, Darby Slick. The other, "White Rabbit", was her own, a two-and-a-half-minute march through Alice's Adventures in Wonderland that built like Ravel's Bolero.

The band went into RCA's studio in Hollywood with producer Rick Jarrard at the end of 1966. They also brought along Jerry Garcia of the Grateful Dead, who played guitar on several tracks, helped with arrangements and was listed on the sleeve as "musical and spiritual adviser". Spencer Dryden, a jazz-minded drummer, had joined that year, and Kaukonen contributed a delicate acoustic instrumental called "Embryonic Journey".

Surrealistic Pillow came out in February 1967, just weeks after the Human Be-In in Golden Gate Park. "Somebody to Love" reached number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 that summer, and "White Rabbit" reached number 8. The album rose to number 3. For many Americans who had never been near Haight-Ashbury, this was the first sound of San Francisco they heard.

The success put Slick at the center of the band, and her voice, sharp and powerful against Balin's tender tenor, became its signature. Over the next few years the Airplane grew louder and more political, on albums such as After Bathing at Baxter's and Volunteers. They played Monterey, Woodstock and Altamont, the three festivals that bracketed the era.

But Surrealistic Pillow is where most listeners met them, and its two hits remain the songs people think of when they think of 1967.

stories.title: The Summer of Love
stories.body:
By the end of 1966, a few blocks of San Francisco around the corner of Haight and Ashbury streets had become the home of a new way of living. Cheap Victorian houses filled with students, artists and musicians. The Grateful Dead lived at 710 Ashbury Street. Jefferson Airplane and Big Brother and the Holding Company were playing the Fillmore Auditorium, run by Bill Graham, and the Avalon Ballroom, run by Chet Helms and the Family Dog, under posters drawn in swirling, nearly unreadable lettering.

On January 14, 1967, at least 20,000 people gathered at the polo field in Golden Gate Park for what organizers called a Human Be-In. Poets Allen Ginsberg and Gary Snyder spoke, Timothy Leary told the crowd to "turn on, tune in, drop out", and the Dead, the Airplane and Quicksilver Messenger Service played. Newspapers across the country covered it, and word spread that something was happening in San Francisco.

That spring, local groups began planning for the young people they expected to arrive once school let out. The Diggers, a community group, handed out free food in the park and ran a free store. In May, Scott McKenzie released "San Francisco (Be Sure to Wear Flowers in Your Hair)", written by John Phillips of the Mamas and the Papas to promote the Monterey Pop Festival in June. It became a worldwide hit and an advertisement for the city.

Tens of thousands came, with estimates reaching as high as 100,000. The neighborhood could not absorb them. Many were teenagers with no money and nowhere to stay. Free clinics opened to treat bad drug reactions and illness, and crime and hard drugs followed the crowds. The music was the best part of it. Big Brother broke through at Monterey, and the Dead and the Airplane played free shows in the Panhandle.

By the fall, many of the people who had built the scene wanted out. On October 2, police raided the Dead's house on Ashbury. Four days later, residents staged a mock funeral procession called "The Death of the Hippie" through the Haight, declaring the whole thing finished.

The Summer of Love lasted only a few months, but the records made by its bands, from Surrealistic Pillow to Cheap Thrills, carried the sound of San Francisco far beyond the city.

stories.title: Barton Hall, May 1977
stories.dek: The Grateful Dead's most famous night
stories.body:
By the spring of 1977 the Grateful Dead had been playing for twelve years, and they had just come back from a break. They had stopped touring in late 1974, retiring the huge Wall of Sound speaker system, and returned to the road in 1976. Their new album, Terrapin Station, was nearly finished, and the band that toured the East Coast in May 1977 was playing as well as it ever had.

On May 8 the tour reached Barton Hall, a field house at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. General admission tickets cost $7.50. The day had started like spring, but the temperature dropped, and by the time fans lined up outside it was snowing, a rare May snowstorm that left people soaked and cold when they came in.

The first set was a run of shorter songs: "New Minglewood Blues", "Loser", "Jack Straw", "Deal" and others, closing with a long, funky "Dancing in the Street". It was the second set that made the night famous. The band opened with "Scarlet Begonias" and slid into "Fire on the Mountain", Jerry Garcia's guitar building patiently over Bill Kreutzmann and Mickey Hart's drums. After "Estimated Prophet" came "St. Stephen", then "Not Fade Away", then back to "St. Stephen".

They closed the set with "Morning Dew", the post-apocalyptic folk song by Bonnie Dobson that they had played since their first album. Garcia sang it softly and then built to a long, climactic solo. Many Deadheads still name it the best version they ever played. The encore was "One More Saturday Night".

The show did not stay in Ithaca for long. Betty Cantor-Jackson, the Dead's longtime recording engineer, had made a soundboard tape of the concert, and copies spread through the band's large network of fan tape traders. The Dead let fans record and trade shows as long as nobody sold the tapes, and over the years the Cornell recording was copied and passed around more than almost any other.

In 2011 the Library of Congress selected it for the National Recording Registry. In May 2017, just before the show's 40th anniversary, the band officially released it as Cornell 5/8/77. The music sounded as good as the legend said, and the fans who had stood in the snow had been right all along.

covers.title: Hey Joe
covers.note: The Leaves had the first release, in late 1965. Hendrix based his slow version on Tim Rose's arrangement, and it was his first single.

covers.title: Morning Dew
covers.note: Dobson wrote it about survivors after a nuclear war and first released it on a 1962 live album. It became one of the Dead's great closers.

covers.title: Me and Bobby McGee
covers.note: Kris Kristofferson wrote it with Fred Foster, but Roger Miller released it first. Joplin's version topped the chart months after her death.

covers.title: She's Not There
covers.note: Santana turned the Zombies' 1964 hit into a Latin rock workout with a long guitar break, and it went top 20 in Britain.

covers.title: Turn On Your Love Light
covers.note: Bland's original was a 1961 R&B hit. Pigpen made it a Dead showcase that could run past 20 minutes.

covers.title: Hush
covers.note: Joe South wrote it and Billy Joe Royal released it first, in 1967. Deep Purple's version reached number 4 in America.
